title: Around the World in Eighty Days
author: Jules Verne
summary: Em 1872, o calmo e misterioso inglês Phileas Fogg aposta toda a sua fortuna que consegue dar a volta ao mundo em apenas oitenta dias. Com seu novo criado francês, Passepartout, ele parte de Londres em navios, trens e até num elefante, enquanto um detetive teimoso o persegue achando que ele é um ladrão de banco. Cada atraso pode custar a aposta, e o relógio nunca para.

chapters.title: The Man Who Was Never Late
paragraphs: In 1872, Mr Phileas Fogg lived at number 7, Savile Row, in London. He was a tall, handsome gentleman of about forty. He was rich, but nobody knew where his money came from. He had no wife and no family. He was always calm, and he was never, ever late.

Every day was the same for Mr Fogg. At exactly half past eleven he left his house and walked to the Reform Club. He ate his lunch there, read the newspapers and played cards with his friends. At midnight exactly he went home to bed.

On the morning of October 2nd, Mr Fogg had no servant. He dismissed his last servant because the man brought him shaving water that was two degrees too cold. A new servant arrived at twenty past eleven. He was a cheerful young Frenchman of about thirty.
“My name is Jean Passepartout,” he said. “I've had many jobs. I was a singer, a circus rider and a fireman. Now I want a quiet life, and people say you are the quietest man in England.”
“Passepartout suits me,” said Mr Fogg. “What time is it?”
Passepartout took a big silver watch from his pocket. “Twenty-two minutes past eleven.”
“Your watch is slow by four minutes,” said Mr Fogg. “It doesn't matter. From this moment you are in my service.” Then he put on his hat and left the house.

Passepartout walked through the house. Everything was clean and in order. On the wall was a list of his duties, with the exact minute for each one. “This is perfect,” he said happily. “Mr Fogg is a machine. I'm going to have a very peaceful life here.”
He was completely wrong.

chapters.title: The Bet
paragraphs: That afternoon at the Reform Club, Mr Fogg's friends were talking about a robbery. Three days before, a thief stole fifty-five thousand pounds from the Bank of England.
“He'll escape,” said Mr Stuart. “The world is very big.”

“It was big once,” said Mr Fogg quietly. “Now it's smaller. A man can travel around it in eighty days.” He showed them the times in the newspaper: from London to Suez, then to Bombay, Calcutta, Hong Kong, Yokohama, San Francisco, New York and back to London.
“Eighty days on paper, maybe,” laughed Stuart. “But you forget bad weather, storms, accidents and trains that are late.”
“I don't forget anything,” said Mr Fogg.
“I bet you four thousand pounds that it's impossible,” said Stuart.

“It's very possible,” answered Mr Fogg. “I'll bet twenty thousand pounds, and I'll do it myself. I'll leave tonight, on the 8.45 train to Dover. Today is Wednesday, October 2nd. I'll be back in this room at 8.45 on Saturday, December 21st. If I'm late, my twenty thousand pounds are yours.”
His friends looked at each other. Twenty thousand pounds was half of his money. The other half he was going to take with him for the journey. They agreed to the bet.
At ten to eight Mr Fogg arrived home. “Passepartout,” he said, “we leave for Dover in ten minutes. We're going around the world.”
Passepartout's mouth fell open. “Around the world?”

“In eighty days. Don't bring any trunks. Just a bag with two shirts and three pairs of stockings. We'll buy clothes on the way.” He gave Passepartout a bag full of banknotes. “Take care of this. There are twenty thousand pounds in it.”
Passepartout almost dropped the bag. At 8.45 exactly, the train left the station. Mr Fogg sat calmly with his travel book. The great journey had begun.

chapters.title: The Detective and the Elephant
paragraphs: At Suez, in Egypt, a small thin man was waiting on the quay. His name was Fix, and he was an English detective. He had a description of the bank robber, and he was watching every passenger.

Passepartout came off the ship to get Mr Fogg's passport stamped. Fix looked at the photograph and description. “It's him!” he thought. “A tall gentleman with lots of money, who is suddenly travelling around the world. He's the thief!” Fix sent a telegram to London for a warrant, because he could not arrest Fogg without it. Then he got on the ship to Bombay.
On the ship Fix became friendly with Passepartout. “Where is your master going?” he asked.
“Around the world in eighty days,” said Passepartout. “It's a bet.” Fix smiled. He did not believe a word.

In Bombay, Passepartout went to see the city. He walked into a beautiful temple, but he did not take off his shoes. Three angry priests attacked him. He escaped and ran to the train with no shoes and no hat.
The train went across India. But after a few days it stopped in the middle of the jungle. “The railway isn't finished,” said the conductor. “It starts again at Allahabad, fifty miles away.”

Mr Fogg did not get angry. He looked for transport and found an elephant called Kiouni. Its owner did not want to sell it. Mr Fogg offered more and more money, and at last he paid two thousand pounds. With a young Indian guide and a friendly English officer, Sir Francis Cromarty, they rode into the forest.
“Two thousand pounds for an elephant!” whispered Passepartout. “My master is mad.”
But Mr Fogg sat on the elephant's back as calmly as he sat in his club.

chapters.title: Aouda
paragraphs: In the forest they heard music and saw a long procession. Priests were leading a young woman. She was beautiful, with fair skin and rich clothes, but she walked like someone in a dream.
“That is Aouda,” said the guide sadly. “Her husband was an old prince, and he died. Tomorrow morning they are going to burn her with his body. It's an old custom called suttee.”
“The poor woman!” said Sir Francis. “They have given her drugs, so she can't fight.”
Mr Fogg looked at his watch. “I have twelve hours to spare,” he said. “Let's save her.”
“But you could die!” said Sir Francis.
“Then I'll die,” said Mr Fogg simply.

That night they tried to get into the temple, but guards stood everywhere. Morning came. The priests carried the young woman to the fire, next to the body of the old prince. The fire began to burn. Mr Fogg was ready to run forward alone.
Suddenly everyone screamed. The dead prince stood up! He took the young woman in his arms, walked through the smoke and came straight towards them. The priests fell on their faces in terror.

“Quick!” said the prince. It was Passepartout! In the dark he put on the old prince's clothes and lay on the fire in his place. They ran to the elephant and escaped into the forest. Behind them came shouts and bullets, but nobody caught them.

When Aouda woke up from the drugs, she was on the train to Calcutta. Sir Francis told her the story. She looked at Mr Fogg with tears of thanks in her eyes. “She can't stay in India,” said Mr Fogg. “They'll find her. She'll come with us to Hong Kong.”

chapters.title: Trouble in Hong Kong
paragraphs: They arrived in Hong Kong by ship. Fix was on the same ship. Hong Kong was British, and he hoped to find his warrant there. But it was not there yet.
“I have to stop Fogg here,” thought Fix. “Tomorrow he'll leave British land, and then I can never arrest him.”

The ship to Yokohama, the Carnatic, was going to leave the next morning. But Passepartout found out that it was going to leave that evening. He wanted to tell his master at once. Fix stopped him and took him to a smoky bar.
“Listen,” said Fix. “I'm a detective. Your master is the bank robber. Help me to keep him here, and you'll get some of the reward money.”
“Mr Fogg is the most honest man in the world!” cried Passepartout angrily. “I'll never help you.”
So Fix gave him drink after drink, and then a pipe of opium. Passepartout fell asleep on the floor and did not tell his master about the ship.

The next morning Mr Fogg and Aouda went to the harbour. The Carnatic was gone, and Passepartout was gone too. But Mr Fogg did not lose his calm. He found a small boat called the Tankadere and offered its captain a lot of money. “Take me to Shanghai,” he said. “The big American ship to San Francisco leaves from there.”

Fix decided to go with them. Mr Fogg politely invited him on the boat. For four days the little boat fought a terrible storm. They arrived just in time to see the American ship leaving Shanghai. The captain fired a gun and raised a flag, and the big ship stopped for them.

And Passepartout? He woke up on the Carnatic and arrived in Yokohama with no money. To buy food, he joined a Japanese circus. Mr Fogg found him there, in the middle of a show, wearing a long false nose. Passepartout was so happy that he ran into the audience, and the whole act fell to the ground.

chapters.title: Across America
paragraphs: The ship crossed the Pacific Ocean and arrived in San Francisco on December 3rd. Fix was still with them. His warrant was no use in America, so now he wanted Mr Fogg to get back to England quickly. There, at last, he could arrest him.

They took the train across America. It was a long journey through the mountains and across the great plains. One day the train had to stop because thousands of buffalo were crossing the line. It waited for three hours. Later, the driver drove at full speed across a weak bridge. A minute after they crossed it, the bridge fell into the river.

Then, one cold morning, a group of Sioux warriors attacked the train. They jumped on the carriages and began to fight with the passengers. Bullets flew everywhere. Passepartout climbed under the train and uncoupled the carriages from the engine, so the train stopped near a fort. Soldiers came and the Sioux rode away.
But Passepartout and two other passengers were missing. The Sioux had taken them prisoner.
Mr Fogg looked at Aouda. “I will find him, alive or dead,” he said. “It is my duty.” He knew that he could lose many hours and maybe the whole bet. But he went with thirty soldiers into the snow.

All day and all night Aouda waited at the station. Fix waited with her. The train went on without them. Then, the next morning, they heard shots in the distance. Mr Fogg came back with the soldiers, and with Passepartout and the two passengers. They were all safe.
“You saved my life,” said Passepartout, and he could say nothing more.

But now they were twenty hours late. There was no train. Then Fix found a man with a sledge with a big sail. The wind pushed it over the snow like a ship on the sea, and they reached Omaha in time for a train to New York.

chapters.title: The Henrietta
paragraphs: They arrived in New York on December 11th, but the ship to Liverpool left forty-five minutes before. Passepartout was in despair. “It's my fault,” he said. “I always cause problems for you.”
Mr Fogg said nothing. He walked along the river and found a small steamship called the Henrietta. Her captain was a rough man called Andrew Speedy.
“I'm going to Bordeaux,” said Speedy. “I never take passengers.”

“Then I'll pay you two thousand dollars each to take us,” said Mr Fogg. Speedy agreed. But when they were at sea, Mr Fogg paid the sailors, and they locked the captain in his cabin. Then Mr Fogg turned the ship towards Liverpool. Speedy shouted and banged on the door all day.
Then there was a new problem. The ship needed coal, and there was not enough. Mr Fogg let Speedy out of his cabin. The captain was red with anger. “You're a pirate!” he shouted.
“Captain,” said Mr Fogg, “I want to buy your ship.”
“What?”
“I'll pay you sixty thousand dollars for it. And then I'm going to burn it.”
Speedy's anger disappeared. The ship was old and was worth much less. “Agreed,” he said with a big smile.

So the sailors burned everything made of wood: the chairs, the doors, the cabins, the masts. The fires under the engine went on, and the ship moved on. When they arrived in Ireland, the Henrietta was only a ship of iron. They took a fast train and a boat, and they reached Liverpool on December 21st at twenty to twelve. London was only six hours away. They had plenty of time.
Then Fix put his hand on Mr Fogg's shoulder. “Phileas Fogg,” he said, “I arrest you in the name of the Queen.”

chapters.title: The Lost Day
paragraphs: Mr Fogg sat calmly in the police station in Liverpool. Time passed. At ten past two, Fix ran into the room. His hair was wild, and he could hardly speak.
“Sir,” he said, “I'm so sorry. It was a terrible mistake. The real thief was arrested three days ago. You are free.”
Mr Fogg looked at the detective. Then, for the only time in his life, he moved quickly. He hit Fix, and the detective fell to the floor. “Good!” cried Passepartout.
They took a special train, but they arrived in London at ten to nine. They were five minutes late. Mr Fogg had lost the bet.
The next day Mr Fogg stayed at home. He was a poor man now. In the evening he spoke to Aouda. “I brought you to England, and now I can't help you,” he said. “I'm sorry.”
Aouda took his hand. “Mr Fogg,” she said, “will you have me as your wife? I don't want your money. I want you.”
Mr Fogg stood up. There was a strange light in his eyes. “I love you,” he said simply.

Passepartout was delighted. He ran to the Reverend to arrange the wedding for the next day, Monday. But the Reverend looked at him in surprise. “Monday? Tomorrow is Sunday,” he said. “Today is Saturday.”
Passepartout ran home faster than he ever ran in his life. They travelled east, towards the sun, and so they gained one day. Nobody noticed it. It was still Saturday, December 21st!
“The club, sir! Quickly! It's only twenty to nine!”
Mr Fogg did not wait. He ran into the street and took a cab. At 8.45 exactly, as the clock struck, the door of the Reform Club opened.
“Here I am, gentlemen,” said Mr Fogg.

He won the bet, but he spent almost all of the money on the journey. It did not matter. He married Aouda, the happiest man in England, and Passepartout was at his side. What did he get from his journey around the world? Nothing, perhaps. But a wonderful wife is worth more than any money.
